summary:
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 authorizes FY2024 funding for Department of Defense military activities, military construction, Department of Energy defense activities, and related national security programs, and prescribes military personnel strengths. It was enacted as Public Law 118-31 on December 22, 2023.

The Act authorizes, through funding tables, $169,169,465,000 for procurement; $145,944,719,000 for research, development, test, and evaluation; $288,822,629,000 for operation and maintenance; $176,765,105,000 for military personnel, including $10,553,456,000 for Medicare-eligible retiree health care contributions; $42,522,145,000 in other authorizations, including $38,303,302,000 for the Defense Health Program; and $15,656,630,000 for military construction. It also authorizes $1,350,694,000 for Maritime Administration programs, including $500,000,000 for the Port Infrastructure Development Program, $318,000,000 for the Maritime Security Program, and $198,500,000 for the U.S. Merchant Marine Academy.

Major procurement provisions authorize multiyear Navy contracts for up to 13 block VI Virginia class submarines beginning in FY2024, up to six Auxiliary Personnel Lighter vessels, and require at least 24 V-22 aircraft upgrades absent a national-security certification. The Act limits retirement or reduction of several aircraft fleets, including F-15E, RQ-4, C-130, B-1, A-10, KC-135, and E-3 aircraft, with specified exceptions. It restricts procurement of certain munition chemical materials from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea by a date set by the Secretary of Defense, no later than September 30, 2028, and authorizes a munitions surge reserve for long-lead components.

Personnel provisions make permanent authority to recall retired members for high-demand, low-density assignments; bar DOD from requiring or prohibiting gender or pronoun identification in official correspondence; restrict certain post-service work for governments of countries of concern unless waived for national security; revise foreign employment approval rules; and create review and communication processes for members separated solely for refusal of COVID-19 vaccination. Compensation provisions expand continuation pay eligibility to begin at 7 years, extend numerous bonuses and special pays through December 31, 2024, authorize a 2024 junior enlisted monthly bonus, revise housing and cost-of-living allowances, and set family separation allowance between $250 and $400.

The Act revises acquisition and industrial-base rules, including extending and restructuring “Never Contract with the Enemy” authorities through December 31, 2033, effective 180 days after enactment; extending temporary inflation-related contract adjustment authority through December 31, 2024; and restricting contracts tied to covered logistics platforms such as LOGINK. It provides $6,000,000,000 in general transfer authority, requires annual reporting on funding changes, mandates independent audits of DOD components for FY2024 and the next nine fiscal years, and requires DOD to receive an unqualified financial statement opinion by December 31, 2028.

It directs major planning and reporting efforts on training ranges, special operations force structure, Marine Corps Force Design 2030, Guam infrastructure, technology release and foreign disclosure, Air Force and Space Force force design through 2050, Indo-Pacific and European missile defense, space-based missile defense, electromagnetic warfare governance, cybersecurity monitoring, Cyber Mission Force resiliency, and artificial intelligence acquisition, bug bounty, watermarking, and strategy. It creates extensive Space Force personnel management authorities for officer promotion, selection, separation, continuation, and retirement.

Foreign policy and security provisions authorize $300,000,000 for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative in each of FY2024 and FY2025 and extend it to December 31, 2026; expand munitions replacement authorities for Ukraine, Taiwan, and Israel; restrict certain New START notifications to Russia absent waiver; require a Black Sea strategy; bar NATO withdrawal without Senate approval or an Act of Congress; and establish or modify Indo-Pacific initiatives concerning campaigning, maritime domain awareness, Taiwan training and assistance, Southeast Asia cyber cooperation, AUKUS administration, and PRC-related studies and restrictions.

Military construction provisions authorize major defense-agency projects, including $885,000,000 at Fort Meade, $257,000,000 at Guantanamo Bay, and $181,764,000 at Ramstein, plus energy resilience projects. They address land withdrawals, conveyances, installation resilience planning, Hawaii utility and housing issues, air purification and sustainable materials pilots, and restrictions on Greenbury Point access.

Other divisions revise federal criminal law on child sex abuse and travel for illicit sexual conduct, charter National American Indian Veterans, expand certain special immigrant visas beginning FY2024, update federal data center requirements through 2026, and establish global corruption reporting. The State Department authorization addresses Foreign Service language training, civil service embassy rotations, workplace reporting and retaliation protections, benefits, recruitment, international-organization internships, ASEAN engagement, infrastructure reporting, special envoy review, and human rights reporting. The Intelligence Authorization provisions establish CIA sexual assault and harassment reporting and investigation systems, require intelligence community guidance on commercial remote sensing and AI use, update PRC technology assessments, require study of civil nuclear energy for intelligence facilities, mandate AI policies, and enact classification reforms for older records and over-classification training.
